title: Review: Hypno5e, Shores of the Abstract Line
contentHtml:
Hypno5e - “Shores of the Abstract Line”
Rating: 7.5/10

Buy on iTunes or
order the CD from the label

    It’s really shaping up to be a year for sprawling, ambitious albums. Between Katatonia’s The Fall of Hearts, Cobalt’s Slow Forever, and now Hypno5e’s Shores of the Abstract Line, it seems there’s no shortage of inspiration in the metal camp and not much keeping these artists from using as much of it up as possible. Good thing, then, that these albums are all turning out to be of more or less excellent quality.

  Of the three, Shores requires the most replay to really “get.” Like The Fall of Hearts, Shores navigates the quiet-to-loud dynamic in a way that feels fresh and challenging despite its reliance on time-tested genre tricks. They just do them really well. While the stylistic corollaries might not be as obvious with Hypno5e as they are with Katatonia, who are still marrying Opeth melodies to the loudest Tool riffs they can find, there’s enough prog and post-rock in Hypno5e’s bones to trace out an ancestry. The songs on Shores generally wind up to climaxes, but not always by way of the meticulous layering we expect of post-rock. Hypno5e’s writing style is more of a series of interruptions, where stargazing acoustics and foreign-language samples will slam into djent riffs and screams as easily as they subsume to patient chords and electronic texturing.

The djent sections are so startlingly “metal” on first listen that their scarcity registers as a disappointment. I found myself waiting for these explosive moments and frowning otherwise, but multiple listens are key to understanding that Hypno5e reserve the metal aspects of their sound for transitions rather than showboat moments. Those nuanced chords, electronics, and samples are the band’s true bread-and-butter. That being the case, “Sea Made of Crosses” may be the most accessible track here for metal listeners since it hews closest to metal convention. It follows a recognizable trajectory toward a guitar-driven denouement, although its last minute or so is taken up by an English-language sample that, I think, is a little more on-the-nose than one might at first realize.
It’s interesting to note that as the album unfolds, vocal duties are handed off quite frequently to multilingual audio samples in French and Spanish as well as English. At times they almost constitute their own vocal “presence,” haunting the background and occasionally manifesting upfront. This seems to be an outgrowth of the album’s theme of “shores,” tangentially reminding me (if I’m allowed to break metal-guy protocol for a second) of Drake’s recent Views. Both albums play like flyovers of various musical spaces, but where Drake boxes his “views” on trap, pop-rap, and dancehall into neat radio singles, Hypno5e prefer to tread a broad range of stylistic ground on each track, making for more complete, rounded movements within the greater arc of the album.
​
Shores of the Abstract Line can get to be overwhelming on behemoths like “Blind Man’s Eye,” whose erratic swings from metal stamp to ambient billow are equally crushing and exhausting. While this is generally the norm for the album, “Tio” stands out as being the sole track that sticks to its Latin-flavored acoustic-ballad format for its full run-time. Its placement smack in the heart of the album isn’t accidental, being the most blatantly emotional piece of music on Shores. While it’s a pleasant change-up, it more importantly provides contrast to its austere surroundings, which would simply be too austere without this song. “Tio” sharply delineates the human element at work within the cavernous progressive metal on display here and balances out the message of the dead-voiced clip on “Sea Made of Crosses,” which suggests that an impersonal relationship between the performer and the audience is the only one that exists. Its heartbreaking cries of “tio!” vault right over the abstract lines of language to insist otherwise.

-Brian L.
